analysis.one_liner: Requires drugmakers to share FDA data with the patent office so drug patents can be more easily challenged.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to make drug patents easier to challenge cleared the Senate health committee in July 2026 with an amendment and now sits on the Senate calendar, awaiting a floor vote that has not been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: When drug companies seek FDA approval for a new drug or biologic, they often tell the patent office a different story than they tell the FDA — presenting analytical and manufacturing data one way to win approval and another way to win a broad patent. This bill requires drugmakers to certify that the information they give the FDA matches what they tell the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office, and to hand over FDA-related information that is material to patentability. It also creates a legal defense for someone accused of infringing a drug patent if the patent owner negligently or intentionally failed to make these disclosures, making it easier to knock out improperly obtained patents and open the door to cheaper generic and biosimilar versions.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and insurers who pay for patented drugs. If improperly obtained patents become easier to challenge, generic and biosimilar competitors can enter sooner, which historically drives prices down sharply once competition begins. Generic and biosimilar manufacturers also benefit from better access to information that shows whether a patent should never have been granted.

how_it_helps.text: Requires drug application sponsors and approved-application holders to certify to the FDA that their patent-related submissions are consistent with what they told the Patent and Trademark Office, closing the gap between the two agencies' records.

Requires drugmakers to submit to the patent office any FDA-related information material to patentability — including statements about analytical data in the chemistry, manufacturing, and controls section and characterizations of prior art — information that can show whether a patent was overbroad.

Creates a defense against patent infringement suits when a patent owner negligently or intentionally failed to disclose required information, giving generic and biosimilar challengers a way to invalidate improperly obtained drug patents.

Preserves trade-secret and confidential-information protections for most material handed to the patent office, while excluding from those protections information the patent office deems necessary for the public to understand the scope of patent claims.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which face new disclosure and certification duties for every applicable patent, an additional legal vulnerability if they fail to disclose, and a higher risk that broad or shaky patents get invalidated — shortening the monopoly periods on which their drug revenues depend.

drawbacks.text: The requirements apply mainly to new applications and patents issued after enactment, so effects on the price of existing medicines would build only gradually over years, not immediately.

The new infringement defense can be triggered by negligent non-disclosure as well as intentional non-disclosure, which could create litigation uncertainty over drug patents where companies acted in good faith but missed something.

Dual filings and certifications to the FDA and the patent office add compliance work for drug developers; the bill itself provides no mechanism to measure whether those costs reduce investment in new medicines.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit for patients is real but indirect: the bill does not cap prices, it targets the paperwork gap that lets drugmakers win and defend broad patents, and it phases in over future applications and patents. The costs are borne by the pharmaceutical industry, with some risk of litigation uncertainty and compliance burden that could modestly affect drug development. On balance this is a targeted transparency fix with modest downside, though its real-world impact depends on regulations the patent office still has to write.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate health committee approved the bill with a substitute amendment in June 2026 and formally reported it in July 2026, placing it on the Senate's general calendar, where it now waits for the majority to schedule a floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Maggie Hassan introduced the bill on August 1, 2025, introduced for herself and Senator Josh Hawley, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
The committee held hearings on the bill on March 19, 2026.

On June 17, 2026, the committee ordered the bill to be reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, and on July 28, 2026 it was formally reported by Senator Cassidy with that amendment.

The reported version keeps the core disclosure-and-certification scheme but adds two changes: the non-disclosure defense is not available to a 'covered foreign person,' and it clarifies trade-secret protections while carving out information the patent office determines the public needs to understand patent claim scope.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 528 and has not received a Senate floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drugmakers are better off so far: their existing patent positions remain untouched while the bill sits unscheduled on the Senate calendar. Patients gain nothing until the Senate actually votes.

for.name: Sen. Maggie Hassan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on August 1, 2025, for herself and Senator Hawley.

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from the start.

for.name: Senate HELP Committee (reported by Sen. Bill Cassidy)
for.role: Committee with jurisdiction over FDA drug law
for.what_they_did: Held hearings in March 2026, ordered the bill reported favorably with a substitute amendment on June 17, 2026, and formally reported it on July 28, 2026, moving it to the Senate calendar.

sides.party_line_note: The bill pairs a Democratic sponsor with a Republican cosponsor, and the Republican-led Senate HELP committee reported it favorably with an amendment; no floor vote has occurred and no opposition appears in the congressional record so far.

industries.note: The bill forces them to hand the patent office FDA-related information that is material to patentability and creates an infringement defense against patents they obtained without full disclosure, raising the risk that broad patents get invalidated and monopoly periods shrink. Their revenue depends on long exclusivity at prices far above generic levels, so their interest in defeating or narrowing the bill runs against patients' interest in cheaper drugs.

Better disclosure gives them more information to challenge weak patents, and the new non-disclosure defense gives them a litigation tool, so they can reach the market sooner — the same outcome that lowers prices for patients.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits on the general Senate calendar, where most reported bills wait indefinitely without a scheduled vote. Its bipartisan sponsorship and a favorable committee report give it a better-than-average path, and it could move as part of a broader health or FDA package, but with no floor date set and no action yet in the House, the likeliest outcome is that it stalls on the calendar unless leadership chooses to spend floor time on it.
